title: 1 Kings 15:25–34
context: In Israel, Jeroboam’s son Nadab reigns two years before Baasha assassinates him and wipes out Jeroboam’s house, fulfilling Ahijah’s word (14:10-11). Baasha then reigns twenty-four years from Tirzah and repeats Jeroboam’s sins. Regnal figures in Kings are commonly thought to involve counting conventions that differ between the kingdoms; such questions are noted with caution.

verses.text: Nadab the son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah; and he reigned over Israel two years.
verses.arminianNotes: Nadab son of Jeroboam reigns two years. Arminian readers note that he receives an opportunity to break from his father’s sins, but does not take it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Nadab’s brief reign is overshadowed by the judgment already pronounced on Jeroboam’s house (14:10-11). The second year of Asa dates his accession to Judah’s calendar.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, and walked in the way of his father, and in his sin with which he made Israel to sin.
verses.arminianNotes: Nadab did evil and walked in his father’s sin. Arminian readers stress that the refrain describes a chosen path, followed freely despite prophetic warning. His brother’s death had already confirmed Ahijah’s word (14:12-18), yet Nadab did not turn.
verses.reformedNotes: The phrase his sin with which he made Israel to sin becomes a recurring refrain. Reformed readers see how a leader’s idolatry corrupts a whole people across generations.

verses.text: Baasha the son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him; and Baasha struck him at Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines; for Nadab and all Israel were besieging Gibbethon.
verses.arminianNotes: Baasha conspires against Nadab and kills him at Gibbethon. Arminian readers note that Baasha’s ambition is his own, even though it serves as the means of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God fulfilling his word through a violent human act. The existing box at Judges 9:23 already discusses how the traditions relate God’s purposes to evil agents, and it applies here.

verses.text: Even in the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha killed him and reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Baasha kills Nadab in Asa’s third year and takes the throne. Arminian readers note how quickly power changes hands when a dynasty rests on rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the northern kingdom, founded in revolt, is now marked by recurring coups. Instability follows unfaithfulness. Gibbethon, a Philistine town, becomes the scene of more than one coup (16:15-17).

verses.text: As soon as he was king, he struck all the house of Jeroboam. He didn’t leave to Jeroboam any who breathed, until he had destroyed him, according to the saying of the LORD, which he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite;
verses.arminianNotes: Baasha destroys all Jeroboam’s house, fulfilling Ahijah’s word. Arminian readers see a sober picture of judgment that had been announced in advance, giving Jeroboam’s house time to repent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the precision of God’s word coming to pass. The prophecy of 14:10-11 is fulfilled exactly, showing that God’s threats are as certain as his promises.

verses.text: for the sins of Jeroboam which he sinned, and with which he made Israel to sin, because of his provocation with which he provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger.
verses.arminianNotes: The reason given is Jeroboam’s sins and his provocation of the LORD. Arminian readers stress that judgment responds to sin freely committed and persisted in.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator explains events theologically: the fall of the house is God’s judgment, not merely political misfortune. Provoked to anger is the narrator’s way of naming covenant breach, not divine caprice.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Nadab, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
verses.arminianNotes: Nadab’s other acts are left to the chronicles of Israel’s kings. Arminian readers note that his reign is remembered chiefly for its spiritual failure. The source citation reminds readers that much more could have been said.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the brief notice reflects the narrator’s priorities. Political details are subordinated to the covenant evaluation. What remains is the verdict of 15:26 and the record of his violent end.

verses.text: There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days.
verses.arminianNotes: The war between Asa and Baasha is mentioned again. Arminian readers see the repetition as framing Baasha’s reign by ongoing conflict with Judah. Asa’s long reign thus spans several northern dynasties.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the narrator’s habit of repeating key facts to link the stories of the two kingdoms. Here it brackets Nadab’s short reign and frames Baasha’s, keeping Judah and Israel side by side in the reader’s view.

verses.text: In the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha the son of Ahijah began to reign over all Israel in Tirzah for twenty-four years.
verses.arminianNotes: Baasha reigns twenty-four years from Asa’s third year. Arminian readers note that a long reign gave Baasha ample opportunity to turn from Jeroboam’s sins. Tirzah, his capital, appears to have been a royal residence since Jeroboam’s day (14:17).
verses.reformedNotes: Elah’s accession in Asa’s twenty-sixth year (16:8) fits this figure if partial years are counted, a convention many interpreters propose. Reformed readers present such reckonings as likely rather than certain.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, and walked in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin with which he made Israel to sin.
verses.arminianNotes: Baasha did evil and walked in Jeroboam’s way. Arminian readers note the tragedy that the man who destroyed Jeroboam’s house repeated Jeroboam’s sin. Seeing judgment fall on another did not lead him to examine his own heart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see how judgment on one sinner does not cure the next. Without a new heart, Baasha follows the same idolatry he had just seen punished.
